The lecture moves from the ecology and classification of arthropod-borne and rodent-borne viruses into the major diseases caused by Flaviviridae, Togaviridae, Filoviridae, and Bunyaviridae. Study Aid — recurring decision chain
Vector or reservoir → identify the transmission pattern.

Arbovirus Foundations

Ecology, classification, life cycle, replication, and general pathogenesis

Arthropod-borne vs rodent-borne viruses p. 1

Arthropod viruses or arboviruses

  • They are an ecologic grouping of viruses whose transmission cycles involve an arthropod vector.
  • A blood-sucking arthropod transmits virus from one vertebrate host to another.
  • The virus multiplies in arthropod tissues without evidence of disease or damage in the vector.
Must Know
The infected arthropod vector acquires a lifelong infection.

Rodent-borne viruses

  • They are maintained in nature by direct rodent-to-rodent transmission without an arthropod vector.
  • Human transmission occurs through contact with rodent body fluids or excretions.

RNA-virus framework used in this lecture p. 2

  • dsRNA, naked: Reoviridae. The lecture marks this as the only dsRNA virus family in its framework.
  • Positive-sense ssRNA, enveloped: Retroviridae, Togaviridae, Flaviviridae, Coronaviridae.
  • Positive-sense ssRNA, naked: Picornaviridae, Caliciviridae, Astroviridae, Hepeviridae.
  • Negative-sense ssRNA, enveloped: Filoviridae, Bunyaviridae, Rhabdoviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Arenaviridae.
  • Retroviridae is highlighted as replicating through a DNA intermediate via reverse transcriptase.
  • Flaviviridae is highlighted as containing major arbovirus diseases worldwide.

ArbovirusDistribution listed in lecture
DengueWorldwide, mainly tropics and subtropics

West Nile virusWorldwide. Same antigenic complex as JEV.

Arbovirus life cycle pp. 2–3

  • Primary vector: mosquito or tick that feeds on an animal host such as birds or rodents.
  • Animal host: reservoir and blood-meal source that helps amplify virus in the population.
  • Bridge vector: another infected mosquito species capable of infecting humans and other mammals.
  • Dead-end or incidental host: humans and other mammals that do not develop enough viremia to pass the virus to additional biting mosquitoes.

Three clinical syndromes p. 3

  1. Fevers of an undifferentiated type: acute febrile illness.
  2. Encephalitis: inflammation of the brain, often with high mortality.
  3. Hemorrhagic fevers: highly severe and potentially fatal.

The lecture links the final clinical syndrome to the degree of viral multiplication and the predominant tissue localization.

Must Know
Because flaviviruses have positive-sense RNA, the genome can be used immediately for translation of structural and non-structural proteins.

General arbovirus pathogenesis p. 3

Insect bite and subcutaneous inoculation
→
Replication in local tissues and regional lymph nodes
→
Primary viremia
→
Delivery to myeloid and lymphoid cells such as monocytes and macrophages
→
Cell lysis and secondary viremia
→
Tropism for liver, brain, vasculature, or skin

Neuroinvasion depends on level of viremia, host genetic background, innate and adaptive immunity, virus strain virulence, and age. Infants and elderly patients are listed as most susceptible.

Dengue Fever

Flaviviridae · Flavivirus

Core identity p. 4

  • Also called breakbone fever because of severe arthralgia.
  • The lecture calls it the most important mosquito-borne viral disease affecting humans.
  • Disease ranges from a nonspecific viral syndrome to severe and fatal hemorrhagic disease.
  • Four distinct serotypes: DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, DEN-4.
  • Infection with one serotype gives lifelong protection against that serotype.
  • Cross-protection between serotypes is short-lived.

Geographic and Philippine epidemiology p. 4

  • An estimated 2.5 billion people live in areas at risk for epidemic transmission.
  • Dengue is endemic in at least 100 countries across Africa, the Americas, parts of the Middle East, Asia, and the Western Pacific.
  • The lecture lists 50–100 million infections annually, around 500,000 DHF cases, and 22,000 deaths, mostly in children.
  • Philippine incidence in the cited study was highest in ages 5–14 years, followed by 0–4 years, then 15–49 years.
  • Highest case fatality was reported in patients under 20 years.
  • 2000–2002: DEN-2 and DEN-1 were more common.
    Later: DEN-3 became more common.
    More recent surveillance in the lecture: DENV-2 and DENV-3 were more common.

Transmission p. 4

  • Primary vector: female Aedes mosquito.
  • Rare routes: vertical transmission, blood transfusion, breast milk, and organ transplant.
Must Know
Only the female mosquito bites in the lecture explanation because the egg-carrying female needs a blood meal for egg development.

Dengue pathophysiology pp. 4–5

Subcutaneous DENV inoculation
→
Replication in macrophages and dendritic cells
→
Spread to lymphatic system
→
Viremia
→
Dissemination to organs
→
Innate and adaptive immune response
Release of inflammatory cytokines
→
Increased vascular permeability
→
Capillary leak
→
Dengue signs and symptoms
Must Know — hallmark
Capillary leak is the hallmark emphasized in the dengue pathophysiology sequence.

Severe dengue and antibody-dependent enhancement p. 5

Initial infection

  • Often mild or asymptomatic.
  • Virus replicates in monocytes or macrophages.
  • T and B lymphocytes are activated.
  • Antibodies bind virus and present it to macrophages, where virus is neutralized or destroyed.

Secondary infection with a different viral type

  • Memory T cells are activated during the second encounter.
  • The lecture describes a suboptimal antibody response that binds virus less effectively and cannot neutralize it efficiently.
  • The antibody-virus complex attaches to Fcγ receptors.
  • This allows more efficient monocyte infection and greater DENV replication.
  • Higher replication increases cytokine release and raises the risk of severe disease.

WHO classification of dengue pp. 5–6

The lecture contrasts the older 1997 classification with the 2009 revised classification by severity. The newer approach separates dengue with or without warning signs from severe dengue.

Probable dengue

Lives in or recently traveled to a dengue-endemic area, has fever, and has at least 2 of the following:

  • Nausea or vomiting
  • Rash
  • Aches and pains
  • Positive tourniquet test
  • Leukopenia
  • Any warning sign

Warning signs

  • Abdominal pain or tenderness
  • Persistent vomiting, described as at least 3 episodes within 24 hours
  • Clinical fluid accumulation such as pleural effusion or ascites
  • Mucosal bleeding
  • Lethargy or restlessness
  • Liver enlargement > 2 cm
  • Rising hematocrit together with a rapid fall in platelet count

Severe dengue

  • Severe plasma leakage: shock or fluid accumulation with respiratory distress.
  • Severe bleeding: as evaluated by the clinician.
  • Severe organ involvement: high AST or ALT, impaired consciousness or behavioral changes, myocarditis, or other organ involvement.
Must Know
If the patient has any one severe-dengue criterion, the lecture states the patient can be tagged as having severe dengue.

Course of dengue illness pp. 6–7

Incubation: 3–14 days after the Aedes bite. Average is 7 days.

Febrile phase

  • Typically 0–7 days. This is the viremic phase.
  • Biphasic fever may occur, but a straight or intermittent fever for 2–7 days can also occur.
  • Defervescence usually occurs between day 3 and day 8 and must be watched for warning signs.
  • Typical manifestations: abrupt high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, transient macular or maculopapular rash, minor hemorrhagic manifestations, facial flushing, injected oropharynx, anorexia.
  • Laboratory clues: leukopenia first, mild to moderate thrombocytopenia, elevated ALT and AST, hyponatremia.

Critical phase

  • Usually starts around defervescence. It may begin as early as day 3 while the patient is still febrile.
  • Usually lasts 24–48 hours.
  • Onset clues: rapid platelet decline with rising HCT, plus warning signs.
  • Laboratory findings: about 20% HCT rise from baseline, moderate to severe thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, transient aPTT increase with decreased fibrinogen.
  • Major complications: hypovolemic shock from plasma leakage, end-organ impairment from prolonged shock, severe hemorrhage, encephalopathy.

Recovery phase

  • Follows the critical phase.
  • Extravasated fluid is gradually reabsorbed over 48–72 hours.
  • Diuresis increases and hemodynamic status stabilizes.
  • Temporary bradycardia can occur while the patient remains hemodynamically stable.
  • A second rash or Herman’s rash may appear, with small circular islands of unaffected white skin and marked pruritus.
  • HCT stabilizes or becomes slightly lower because of hemodilution.
  • WBC recovers first, then platelets rise afterward.
Must Know — critical phase
The critical phase is the time when the lecture says the patient needs close monitoring.
Both the critical and recovery phases are described as non-viremic.
Must Know — CBC trend
WBC and platelet counts fall because of bone marrow suppression and some degree of capillary permeability.

Dengue hemorrhagic fever p. 7

  • The lecture notes this as a severe syndrome associated with preexisting non-neutralizing heterologous dengue antibody, including passively acquired maternal antibody or prior infection with a different serotype.
  • Initial symptoms resemble ordinary dengue before the condition worsens.
  • Key pathologic feature: increased vascular permeability with plasma leakage into interstitial spaces, associated with increased vasoactive cytokines.
  • This can lead to life-threatening shock.
Dengue diagnostic timeline
TypeTestLecture timingKey notes
MolecularRT-PCRFirst 0–7 daysConfirmatory. Not readily available in many hospitals according to the lecture.
AntigenNS1First 0–7 daysReadily available in hospitals in the lecture.
SerologyIgM, IgGAfter day 3Serology is not recommended in the acute phase in the lecture. Some books cited in the lecture place positivity around day 5–7.

Serology details p. 7

IgM

  • May cross-react with other flaviviruses.
  • Can persist for 3 months or longer.
  • Seroconversion in paired samples supports current infection.
  • Compatible symptoms plus IgM positivity is presented as a definitive diagnosis in the lecture.

IgG

  • Seroconversion in paired samples supports current infection.
  • Appears around the 4th–5th day in the lecture notes.
  • Not recommended for the acute phase. It can help indicate previous exposure or vaccination.

Treatment p. 7

  • No antiviral drug therapy for dengue fever.
  • Fluid replacement is the key management measure.
  • Blood transfusion is no longer encouraged routinely. It is used as needed for severe bleeding, rapid fall in Hb and HCT, or very low platelets.
  • Acetaminophen or paracetamol may be used for fever and pain.
  • Avoid NSAIDs because of bleeding risk.

Prevention and control pp. 7–8

The lecture gives two pillars: vector control and vaccination.

  • Environmental management and removal of artificial mosquito habitats.
  • Proper solid-waste disposal and weekly covering, emptying, and cleaning of domestic water storage containers.
  • Insecticide use for adult mosquito control and water storage containers.
  • Household protection such as screens, coils, and vaporizers.
  • Long sleeves and pants in heavily infested areas.
  • Community participation, outbreak space spraying, and active vector surveillance.
Dengue vaccines taught in the lecture
FeatureCYD-TDV · DengvaxiaTAK-003 · Qdenga
Dose0.5 mL0.5 mL
Schedule3 doses, 6 months apart2 doses, 3 months apart
Indication in lecturePrevention in ages 9–45 with laboratory-confirmed prior dengue infection and living in endemic areas.Prevention from age 4 in the European Union or age 6 in Indonesia.
Contraindication or restriction highlightedNo previous dengue exposure because of higher severe-dengue risk.None specified during the lecture.
Pre-vaccination screeningYesNo
Genomic backboneYellow feverDENV-2
Must Know — CYD-TDV
CYD-TDV is described as efficacious and safe in people with a previous dengue infection.
The lecture warns of an increased risk of severe dengue when a person’s first natural dengue infection occurs after vaccination.
Pre-vaccination screening is therefore recommended when considering a Dengvaxia program.
Must Know — TAK-003
The DENV-2 genomic backbone is taught as making the immune response more robust.
The lecture states that WHO does not recommend routine screening for previous dengue infection before TAK-003.
Lecture-Specific Note
The lecture states that the dengue vaccines discussed were not licensed in the Philippines at the time of the lecture.

Japanese Encephalitis Virus

Flaviviridae · Flavivirus

Core identity p. 8

  • Related to Dengue, Yellow fever, and West Nile viruses.
  • The lecture identifies JEV as the leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia.
  • Found mainly in Southeast Asian countries. The Philippines is described as endemic.
  • The lecture lists 24 countries at risk and 3 billion people at risk.

Epidemiology pp. 8–9

  • Transmission occurs mainly in rural agricultural areas associated with rice production and flood irrigation.
  • Temperate regions: peaks in summer and fall.
  • Tropics and subtropics: occurs year-round, often peaking during the rainy season.
  • The lecture lists about 100,000 clinical cases per year.
  • Philippine data in the lecture: 7–18% of meningitis and encephalitis cases and 16–40% of clinical encephalitic cases were attributed to JE in cited studies.
  • JEV surveillance showed presence in all regions, with suspected and confirmed cases across multiple provinces.
  • Age is strongly pediatric in the cited data. Confirmed cases were predominantly under 15 years.
Must Know
Rice production, flood irrigation, and the rainy season favor proliferation of the mosquito vector.

Transmission cycle p. 9

  • Vectors: Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnui groups.
  • Natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts: pigs and wading or water birds.
  • Incidental or dead-end hosts: humans and horses.
  • Humans and horses do not reach the high viremia needed to continue mosquito transmission.

Clinical manifestations p. 9

  • Incubation: 5–15 days.
  • Clinical spectrum: simple febrile illness, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis with behavioral changes, and polio-like acute flaccid paralysis.
  • Case fatality rate given in the clinical section: 5–30%.
  • Among survivors, 30–50% may have lasting CNS damage.

Diagnosis p. 9

  • Use CSF or serum to detect JEV-specific IgM by ELISA.
  • If negative, a convalescent sample may be tested after about 10–14 days of acute illness.
  • A rise in IgM ELISA titers supports a recent JE infection.

Treatment and prevention p. 9

  • No antiviral therapy.
  • Supportive care and management of complications.
  • Vector control and personal protective measures.
  • Mass immunization of children and pigs is recommended in endemic areas in the lecture.
  • Vaccination of travelers to endemic areas. Both inactivated and live-attenuated vaccines are listed as available.

Yellow Fever

Flaviviridae · Flavivirus

Core identity and epidemiology pp. 9–10

  • Single serotype with 7 genotypes.
  • Acute febrile illness in tropical and subtropical areas of Africa and South America.
  • Severe cases feature liver dysfunction, renal dysfunction, and hemorrhage.
  • The lecture estimates about 200,000 infections and 30,000 deaths per year worldwide.
  • Around 90% of cases are listed as occurring in Africa.
Two major epidemiologic cycles of Yellow Fever
FeatureUrban Yellow FeverJungle Yellow Fever
Primarily affectsHumansMonkeys
VectorsAedes aegyptiHaemagogus and Aedes
Typical settingHuman settlementsMoist forest canopy
Transmission emphasisPerson-to-person transmission through domestic Aedes mosquitoes.Primarily a monkey disease. Humans can be infected during forest exposure such as clearing activities.

Pathogenesis p. 10

Bite of infected Aedes
→
Virus inoculated into host
→
Replication in dendritic cells
→
Regional lymph nodes
→
Replication in macrophages or monocytes
→
Lymphatic and bloodstream spread
Spread to liver, spleen, kidney, bone marrow, myocardium
→
Eosinophilic degeneration, apoptosis, fatty change
→
Necrosis and degenerative change
→
Liver damage, renal failure, cerebral edema, systemic inflammatory response

The lecture links systemic inflammatory injury of the myocardium to eventual shock.

Clinical presentation p. 10

Incubation: 3–6 days.

Viremic phase

  • Fever, chills, headache, dizziness, myalgia, backache, nausea, vomiting, and bradycardia.
  • Most patients recover at this point.
  • Around 15% progress to severe disease in the lecture.

Severe disease or hepatorenal failure

  • Fever, jaundice, renal failure, hemorrhage, myocarditis, CNS dysfunction.
  • Mortality is described as high, about 20% once severe disease is reached.
  • Severe disease is noted especially in young children and elderly adults, usually around day 7–10.
  • Encephalitis is rare.
  • The lecture contrasts Yellow fever with JE by stating that patients either die or recover completely, without the neurologic sequelae commonly emphasized for JE.

Laboratory diagnosis p. 10

  • Viral detection or isolation: immunohistochemistry, ELISA, PCR, or recovery from blood during the first 4 days after symptom onset.
  • IgM: usually appears during the first week. Detection by ELISA gives a presumptive diagnosis.
  • Confirmation: four-fold or greater rise in antibody titers between acute and convalescent phases.

Treatment and prevention pp. 10–11

  • No antiviral therapy. Treatment is supportive.
  • 17D strain live attenuated vaccine is taught as the most effective preventive measure.
  • Recommended for travelers to endemic areas and residents of endemic regions.
  • Contraindications listed in the lecture: under 9 months, pregnancy, egg allergy, immunocompromised state.

Zika Virus

Flaviviridae · Flavivirus

Core identity and epidemiologic timeline p. 11

  • Primary mosquito vector: Aedes aegypti.
  • Most severe complication: Congenital Zika Syndrome.
  • First identified in the Zika forest in Uganda in 1947.
  • Reported in 86 countries in the lecture and widely distributed in Asia, Africa, Micronesia, and South and Central America.
  • 2007: first large human outbreak on Yap Island in Micronesia.
  • March 2015: outbreak of rash illness reported in Brazil.
  • July 2015: association with Guillain-Barre Syndrome.
  • October 2015: association between infection and microcephaly confirmed.

Transmission p. 11

  • Primarily through the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito.
  • Other routes: vertical transmission, sexual contact, blood transfusion, organ transplantation.

Pathophysiology p. 11

Bite of infected Aedes
→
Virus inoculates keratinocytes in skin
→
Virus moves to lymph nodes
→
Viremia
→
Spread to different organ systems

In congenital Zika, the virus infects fetal neural progenitor cells, resulting in microcephaly.

Clinical presentation p. 11

  • Incubation: 3–14 days.
  • Majority are asymptomatic.
  • Nonspecific symptoms: fever, rash, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, headache lasting about 2–7 days.
  • Potential complications: meningoencephalitis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre Syndrome.
  • Transverse myelitis and Guillain-Barre Syndrome may present with acute flaccid paralysis.

Congenital Zika Syndrome

  • Subcortical calcifications
  • Microcephaly
  • Ventriculomegaly
  • Ocular deficits
  • Spasticity
  • Seizures
Zika diagnostic timing
Illness timingTestWhat is detected
0–14 daysPCR from blood or urineZika RNA
>14 daysSerologyIgM antibodies

Treatment and prevention p. 11

  • No antiviral therapy.
  • Symptomatic management with IV hydration and acetaminophen for fever and joint pain.
  • No vaccine available in the lecture.
  • Vector control and personal protective measures.
  • Safe sex practices because Zika can be sexually transmitted.
  • Abstinence during pregnancy is listed as a preventive measure.

Chikungunya

Togaviridae · Alphavirus

Core identity p. 11

  • Only virus from Togaviridae included among the major arboviruses in this lecture.
  • The name comes from the Kimakonde language and means “to become contorted”, referring to the stooped posture caused by arthralgia.
  • First recognized in 1952 during an outbreak in southern Tanzania.
  • Symptoms may resemble Dengue and Zika.
  • Most outbreaks occur in Africa and Southeast Asia, with reports across more than 60 countries.
Must Know — hallmark
Joint pain is the hallmark of Chikungunya in the lecture.

Vector and transmission pp. 11–12

  • Primarily from the bite of an infected female Aedes mosquito.
  • Sylvatic cycle: monkeys.
  • Urban cycle: humans.
  • Rare vertical transmission and blood transfusion transmission are listed.

Pathophysiology p. 12

Mosquito bite
→
Replication in dermal fibroblasts
→
Entry into bloodstream
→
Direct invasion and replication in joints and muscles
→
Dissemination to liver, brain, lymphoid tissue

Chronic joint disease occurs in up to 60% in the lecture. Proposed contributors are persistent viral replication, continued immune response to remaining RNA, and autoimmunity.

Clinical presentation p. 12

Fever

  • Abrupt onset.
  • Usually high-grade.

Rash

  • Appears near the end of the febrile phase, around day 3–5.
  • Maculopapular, diffuse, irritating, and itchy.
  • Common on arms, back, and shoulders.
  • Lasts up to 48 hours.

Arthralgia

  • Polyarticular, affecting 5 or more joints.
  • Commonly ankle, knee, wrist, and hand joints.
  • Typically bilateral and symmetric.

Diagnosis p. 12

  • IgM: seen from day 5 and may persist up to 3 months.
  • IgG: noted by about 2 weeks after symptom onset.
  • RT-PCR.
  • Viral culture is rarely done because of unavailability.
  • Laboratory clues: lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia.

Treatment p. 12

  • No antiviral therapy.
  • Hydration and analgesics for joint pain.
  • Post-acute disease: acetaminophen or NSAIDs.
  • Short course of steroids for synovitis or severe joint pain.
  • Symptoms lasting 3 months or longer: DMARDs such as methotrexate and sulfasalazine may be given.

Prevention p. 12

  • No vaccine available in the lecture.
  • Vector control.
  • Personal protective measures.

Cross-Arbovirus Disease Patterns

Disease mechanisms of flaviviruses and togaviruses

Pattern recognition p. 12

  • Encephalitis: St. Louis encephalitis, West Nile encephalitis, Eastern equine encephalitis, and Japanese encephalitis are specifically listed. Dengue may also present with encephalitis.
  • Hepatitis: more commonly seen with Dengue and Yellow fever because of liver tropism.
  • Flaviviruses can infect cells of the monocyte-macrophage lineage.
  • They establish viremia and systemic infection.
  • They are good inducers of interferons and cytokines, helping account for flu-like symptoms.
Must Know — shock mechanism
Non-neutralizing antibody can enhance flavivirus infection through Fc receptors. This is antibody-dependent enhancement and can produce more severe disease.

Filoviridae

Ebolavirus and Marburgvirus

Taxonomy and basic features pp. 12–13

Filoviruses are taught as causes of African hemorrhagic fever.

Ebolavirus species listed

  • Bundibugyo
  • Zaire
  • Sudan
  • Tai Forest
  • Bombali
  • Reston, noted as not causing disease in humans

Marburgvirus

  • Marburg

Virion properties

  • Single-stranded RNA, negative sense, nonsegmented.
  • Filamentous or thread-like, pleomorphic morphology. Shapes may include 6-shaped, U-shaped, or circular forms.
  • Helical nucleocapsid.
  • Lipid membrane envelope.
  • Surface glycoprotein spikes are trimers around 10 nm long.
Must Know — unusual coding strategy
The lecture highlights an unusual Ebolavirus strategy in which the envelope glycoprotein is encoded in two reading frames and requires transcriptional editing or translational frame shifting for expression.

Marburg epidemiology p. 13

  • First discovered in 1967 among laboratory workers exposed to tissues of African green monkeys.
  • The monkeys had been imported to Germany and Yugoslavia.
  • Antibody surveys cited in the lecture suggested presence in East Africa.
  • Outbreaks are listed in Kenya, South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Angola.

Ebola epidemiology p. 13

  • 1976: two simultaneous hemorrhagic-fever outbreaks in Sudan and Zaire.
  • 1989: Reston ebolavirus found in macaque monkeys in Reston, Virginia. The monkeys originated from the Philippines.
  • 1994: Tai Forest ebolavirus recognized after a scientist became ill following an autopsy on a chimpanzee.
  • 2007: Bundibugyo ebolavirus isolated during an outbreak in Uganda.
  • 2018: Bombali ebolavirus detected in free-tailed bats in Sierra Leone.
  • Large EVD outbreaks are associated in the lecture with Bundibugyo, Zaire, and Sudan ebolaviruses.
  • Since 2008, Reston virus has been detected in pigs in China and the Philippines without reported human illness or death.
  • In 2009, six people in the Philippines were antibody-positive after contact with sick pigs but had no significant symptoms.

Reservoir, hosts, and ecology p. 13

  • The reservoir is not completely known.
  • The lecture identifies fruit bats as possible natural hosts and describes an enzootic bat cycle.
  • Non-human primates such as chimpanzees and gorillas can become infected after contact with bats or secretions.
  • Primates and humans are described as accidental hosts in the ecology discussion.
  • The lecture summary also notes suspected reservoirs as bats or possibly rodents.
Must Know — entry into human populations
Ebola is introduced through close contact with blood, secretions, organs, or other body fluids of infected animals.

Human transmission p. 13

  • Direct contact with infected body fluids.
  • Fomites.
  • Sexual contact.
  • Primate-to-human transmission through infected body fluids.
  • Possible fruit bat-to-human transmission.

Ebola pathophysiology p. 14

Virus enters through skin or mucosa
→
Targets macrophages and dendritic cells
→
Replication and cell death
→
Virion release
→
Spread to regional lymph nodes
→
Systemic spread to hepatocytes, endothelial cells, macrophages in lymphoid tissue

The lecture links this spread to marked cytokine dysregulation and coagulopathy.

Clinical manifestations p. 14

Incubation: EVD 2–21 days. MVD 5–10 days.

Key Differentiator
EVD and MVD have very similar presentations and may be difficult to distinguish clinically.

Initial nonspecific illness

  • High fever, chills, headache, body pain, joint pain, fatigue, pharyngitis, abdominal pain, profuse watery diarrhea.
  • Nausea and vomiting, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash.

Later severe disease

  • Dehydration leading to hypotension.
  • Bleeding.
  • Altered mental state and seizures.
  • Bradycardia and respiratory compromise.
  • Hepatitis and renal failure.
  • Shock.

After recovery

  • Visual problems such as cataract or uveitis.
  • Hearing loss.
  • Cognitive changes.
  • Joint pain.
  • Relapse.

Diagnosis p. 14

  • PCR is the most commonly used definitive test in the lecture and detects viral RNA.
  • PCR is the test of choice because of higher sensitivity than serology.
  • Antigen detection by ELISA.
  • Serology by ELISA or indirect fluorescence antibody.

Treatment p. 14

  • No specific antiviral therapy is listed.
  • Management is primarily supportive.
  • For EVD: monoclonal antibodies.
  • Convalescent plasma is listed with unclear benefit.

Prevention and control p. 14

  • Raise awareness of risk factors.
  • Protective clothing when handling suspected animals.
  • Appropriate PPE when caring for ill patients.
  • Standard precautions for all patients regardless of diagnosis.
  • Adequate laboratory staff training.
  • Vaccination.

Bunyaviridae and Hantavirus

Rodent-borne disease focus

Bunyaviridae basics p. 14

  • Also referred to as Bunyavirales in the lecture.
  • Five genera listed: Orthobunyavirus, Hantavirus, Nairovirus, Phlebovirus, Tospovirus.
  • Virion properties: negative-sense ssRNA, enveloped, spherical, triple-segmented genome.
Must Know
Hantavirus is the most significant rodent-borne virus emphasized in the lecture and can cause Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome.

Hantavirus species and disease associations p. 15

  • Sin Nombre virus: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome or cardiopulmonary syndrome.
  • Other HPS-associated viruses listed: New York virus, Black Creek Canal virus, Bayou virus.
  • Hantaan and Dobrava viruses: severe HFRS in Asia and Europe.
  • Seoul virus: moderate HFRS in Eurasia.
  • Puumala virus: mild nephropathia epidemica, prevalent in Scandinavia.

Epidemiology, reservoir, and transmission p. 15

  • Found worldwide. The lecture lists 100,000–200,000 annual cases.
  • China is reported as having the highest annual incidence of hantavirus-related diseases.
  • Primary reservoir: rodents.
  • Peromyscus maniculatus, the deer mouse, is the primary Sin Nombre reservoir in the USA.
  • Transmission: inhalation of contaminated feces, saliva, or urine. Rodent bite. Direct contact of nose or mouth with contaminated material. Ingestion of contaminated material.
  • Each hantavirus is associated with a specific rodent host.
  • Rodent infection is lifelong and does not cause deleterious effects in the rodent.

Management p. 15

  • Primarily supportive.
  • Cardiorespiratory support.
  • Fluid balance.
  • Dialysis as indicated.
  • Ribavirin may be of some benefit for HPS according to the lecture.

Prevention p. 15

  • Rodent control.
  • Avoid rodent contact.
  • Appropriate cleanup of nesting sites.
  • No vaccine available.

Cram Sheet

Fastest final recall

Red-flag lecture points
Arbovirus vectors can acquire lifelong infection.
Humans are usually accidental hosts, except urban Yellow fever and Dengue in the lecture.
Flavivirus positive-sense RNA can be translated immediately.
Dengue hallmark: capillary leak.
Chikungunya hallmark: joint pain.
Hantavirus can cause HPS and HFRS.
Ebola and Marburg cause African hemorrhagic fevers.

Dengue in 60 seconds

  • 4 serotypes: DEN-1 to DEN-4.
  • Vector: female Aedes.
  • Severe dengue mechanism: ADE via Fcγ receptors in a secondary infection with a different type.
  • Warning trend: HCT up + platelets rapidly down.
  • Critical phase: about 24–48 h around defervescence.
  • Severe criterion present? Any one is enough in the lecture.
  • 0–7 d: RT-PCR or NS1.
  • Later: IgM or IgG.
  • Treatment: fluids. Paracetamol. Avoid NSAIDs.

Dengue phase memory

  • Febrile: viremic. WBC drops first.
  • Critical: non-viremic. HCT rises, platelets fall, plasma leak risk.
  • Recovery: non-viremic. Fluid reabsorbs over 48–72 h. WBC rises first, platelets follow.
  • Study Aid: “WBC first down, first back up” reflects the lecture’s CBC sequence.
Arbovirus one-line cues
VirusIf you see this, think…Vector or host anchor
DengueCapillary leak, rising HCT, falling platelets, hemorrhage or shockFemale Aedes
JEVLeading viral encephalitis cause in Asia, pediatric pattern, possible lasting CNS damageCulex · pigs and wading birds amplify · humans and horses dead-end
Yellow feverJaundice + renal failure + hemorrhageAedes in urban cycle · monkeys in jungle cycle
ZikaPregnancy + microcephaly or congenital neurologic findingsAedes · vertical and sexual transmission also taught
ChikungunyaBilateral symmetric polyarthralgia and chronic joint diseaseAedes · monkeys sylvatic · humans urban

JEV

  • Vector: Culex tritaeniorhynchus / vishnui.
  • Amplifiers: pigs + wading birds.
  • Dead-end: humans + horses.
  • Incubation: 5–15 d.
  • Dx: JEV IgM ELISA in CSF or serum.
  • No antiviral. Supportive care. Vaccine available.

Yellow Fever

  • Incubation: 3–6 d.
  • Severe: hepatorenal failure, jaundice, hemorrhage, myocarditis, CNS dysfunction.
  • Early viral recovery: first 4 d.
  • IgM: first week.
  • Vaccine: 17D live attenuated.
  • Contra: under 9 months, pregnancy, egg allergy, immunocompromised.

Zika

  • Most are asymptomatic.
  • Congenital syndrome: microcephaly, subcortical calcifications, ventriculomegaly, ocular deficits, spasticity, seizures.
  • 0–14 d: PCR blood or urine.
  • After 14 d: IgM.
  • No vaccine in lecture.

Chikungunya

  • Joint pain = hallmark.
  • Arthralgia: 5+ joints, often ankle, knee, wrist, hand, bilateral and symmetric.
  • IgM from day 5, may persist 3 months.
  • IgG around 2 weeks.
  • Symptoms ≥3 months: DMARDs such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine may be used.
Dengue vaccine trap
CYD-TDV: prior dengue infection matters. The lecture warns of severe-dengue risk in those without prior exposure.
TAK-003: DENV-2 genomic backbone. Routine prior-infection screening is not recommended in the lecture.
